428.title: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 90)
428.hook: a thousand years are like yesterday; teach us to count our days
428.howItsDone: Psalm 90 is often read at Christian funerals and on New Year's Eve, and Isaac Watts's hymn based on it, "O God, Our Help in Ages Past," is sung at memorials and remembrance services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a nest by the altar, and your line, even the sparrow has a home.

Some people keep a jar of marbles on a shelf: one for every Saturday they might reasonably have left, worked out from their age. Every Saturday morning, they take one out and drop it in a bowl. It sounds grim. Some who try it say the opposite: the shrinking jar makes the Saturdays better. They stop wasting them. That idea is very old. A psalm whose heading carries the name of Moses is about exactly this: the shortness of a life held against the length of God, and a request to learn how to count.
screen: `A JAR OF MARBLES.` → `ONE FOR EACH SATURDAY LEFT.` → `A PRAYER OF MOSES.`

segments.voice: The heading reads, "A Prayer of Moses the man of God." It starts with God's size: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations." Before the mountains were born, you were God. Then it zooms out until time itself shrinks: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night." A watch was a few hours of guard duty. A thousand years, gone like a night shift. Next to that, human life looks like grass, the psalm says, green in the morning and cut down by evening. It even gives a number: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten." Seventy. Eighty, if strong. "For it is soon cut off, and we fly away." This could have ended in gloom. Instead it turns into a request. "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." To number is to count, the way you'd count coins. The same root shows up in the writing on the wall in the book of Daniel: mene, numbered. The psalm doesn't ask to be spared the counting. It asks to be taught to count well, so the counting turns into wisdom instead of fear. And the last verse asks for something lasting: "establish thou the work of our hands." Isaac Watts turned this psalm into a hymn, now usually sung as O God, Our Help in Ages Past, and it's still sung at funerals and remembrance services.
screen: `A THOUSAND YEARS LIKE YESTERDAY` · `THREESCORE YEARS AND TEN` · `TEACH US TO COUNT, NOT TO FEAR` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS` · then, large: `SO TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.`

segments.voice: Count the days left in this month, on your fingers if you like, and hold the number. Then let a few of those days come to mind one at a time, not as a to-do list, and ask of each: what would make this day worth keeping? If you pray, say the psalm's line, so teach us to number our days; if you don't, just hold the number gently, without panic.
Mene. The word numbered from the writing on the wall in Daniel, sharing its root with this psalm's prayer to count our days well.
Your line: number our days. Counted well, they turn into wisdom, not fear. See you tomorrow.

429.title: Under his wings (Psalm 91)
429.hook: he shall cover you with his feathers
429.carry: warm and dark and loud with heartbeats
429.howItsDone: Psalm 91 is a night psalm for many Christians: it is prayed at Compline in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, and many people pray it for protection before travel, surgery or military service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mene, numbered, from the writing on the wall, and your line, number our days.

A shadow crosses the farmyard: a hawk, circling low. The hen doesn't run. She makes one sharp sound, and every chick within earshot comes skittering across the dirt and disappears under her. In two seconds there's no chick to be seen, only a hen who suddenly looks twice her size, feathers puffed, eyes on the sky. Underneath, it's warm and dark and loud with heartbeats. The writers of the Bible had seen it too, and they used it for God, in a psalm said at night.
screen: `A HAWK'S SHADOW.` → `THE HEN CALLS.` → `NO CHICKS IN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty." Then, verse four: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust." The Hebrew word for wing is kanaf. It also means the edge of a cloak. In the book of Ruth, Boaz blesses Ruth, the foreigner who has come to Israel, as one who has come to trust under the wings of the God of Israel. Later, at night, Ruth asks Boaz to spread his kanaf, his cloak, over her, and the King James Bible translates it skirt. Wings and a cloak: both are ways of saying you're covered, you belong. The psalm goes on: "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day." That's one reason it belongs to the night. It is part of Jewish bedtime prayers, and some churches pray it at Compline, the last service of the day. But the psalm can be misused. In the Gospels, when the devil tempts Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, he quotes this very psalm: he shall give his angels charge over thee. Go on, jump. And Jesus answers, "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." The psalm is a place to hide, not a dare to take. And Jesus used the same farmyard picture himself, over Jerusalem: how often would I have gathered thy children together, "even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who could use covering right now, someone traveling, someone sick, someone scared, a kid walking into a hard week, and picture where they are. If you pray, ask God to cover them with his feathers, or simply say their name to God and leave it there. If you don't, hold them in mind and wish them safe, steadily, the way a hen sits still.
Kanaf. Hebrew for wing, also the edge of a cloak, Psalm ninety-one's picture of God as a bird sheltering its young, a psalm for the night.
Your line: warm and dark and loud with heartbeats. Covered, the way a hen covers her chicks. Day four hundred twenty-nine, done.

430.title: Sing a new song (Psalm 96)
430.hook: let the fields be joyful and the trees sing
430.tomorrow: bless the Lord, O my soul
430.howItsDone: Psalm 96 is sung in many churches at Christmas and other feasts, and Christians often take its call to "sing a new song" as a reason to write new hymns and worship music for each generation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kanaf, and your line, warm and dark and loud with heartbeats.
screen: `WARM AND DARK AND LOUD WITH HEARTBEATS.`

segments.voice: When did you last sing something for the first time? Not the chorus stuck in your head since the drive to work. Not the birthday song, or the hymn you could sing in your sleep. Something new in your own mouth. For most adults, it's been years, and there's comfort in the familiar. But the Psalms keep asking for something else. Again and again: sing a new song. And Psalm ninety-six doesn't stop at people. By the end, the fields, the sea and the trees are singing too.
screen: `THE SAME CHORUS, AGAIN.` → `WHEN DID YOU LAST SING SOMETHING NEW?` → `EVEN THE TREES JOIN IN.`

segments.voice: Psalm ninety-six opens, in the King James Bible: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth." That phrase, a new song, turns up in several psalms, in the prophet Isaiah, and then twice in Revelation, the Bible's last book, where it's still being called new. So new here doesn't mean the latest hit. In the Psalms, a new song usually answers something new God has done: a rescue, a victory, a homecoming. Fresh mercy deserves fresh words. And this new song isn't for one nation. All the earth. The psalm tells the families of the peoples to give glory, and it says the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens. Then the song spreads beyond people altogether. "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice." Why are the trees so happy? The last verse says: "For he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth." That sounds alarming, but listen to how it ends: "he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth." In the Psalms, judgment often means setting things right. The trees cheer because justice is finally coming. And this psalm has a second home. Most of it appears again in First Chronicles, in the song sung when David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem.
screen: `NEW SONG, FROM PSALMS TO REVELATION` · `FRESH MERCY, FRESH WORDS` · `THE FIELDS AND TREES REJOICE` · `JUDGMENT: THINGS SET RIGHT` · then, large: `O SING UNTO THE LORD A NEW SONG.`

segments.voice: Take the psalm's first line, O sing unto the Lord a new song, and give it a tune that didn't exist a minute ago: hum it first, then try the words; three notes, off key, it doesn't matter. If you'd rather, sing a hymn or a song you've never sung aloud before. If you pray, let it be your prayer; if you don't, let it be a small act of courage, and rest in the quiet after.

Your line: a new song. Even the trees get a part. That's day four hundred thirty.

431.title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 103)
431.hook: he knows our frame; he remembers we are dust
431.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 103 as a prayer of thanksgiving, and it is sung in hymns such as Henry Francis Lyte's "Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven."

segments.voice: Yesterday, chadash, new, with the trees joining in, and your line, a new song.

Memory is strangely lopsided. A teacher's sharp comment in seventh grade: still there, word for word, decades later. The stranger who held a door when your arms were full of groceries last Tuesday: gone by Wednesday. Memory keeps the wounds on file and lets the kindnesses slip through. It isn't a moral failing exactly; memory seems to keep watch for threats. But left alone, it can make a life look harder than it was. Psalm one hundred three opens with a person giving their own soul a firm reminder, almost a nudge in the ribs. Don't forget.
screen: `THE SHARP COMMENT: KEPT.` → `THE HELD DOOR: FORGOTTEN.` → `A NUDGE TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred three begins, in the King James Bible: "Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." Like the deer psalm, the writer is talking to himself. But this time it isn't comfort. It's a reminder. Then he counts the benefits out loud, one after another: who forgives, who heals, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with lovingkindness, who renews your youth like the eagle's. And this psalm doesn't ask for anything. No request, no complaint, from beginning to end. It just remembers. "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." East and west never meet; you can travel east forever. "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust." Frame is how a person is put together, what they're made of. God knows people are breakable, the psalm says, and is gentle about it. Human days are like grass: the wind passes over, and the place forgets them. And then the turn: "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting." People forget. God remembers that we are dust, and remembers mercy. By the end the psalm calls on the angels, every work of God, and finally its own soul again. Henry Francis Lyte turned it into a hymn, Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven, and churches still sing it.
screen: `TALKING TO YOUR OWN SOUL` · `COUNTING THE BENEFITS` · `AS FAR AS EAST FROM WEST` · `HE KNOWS WE ARE DUST` · then, large: `FORGET NOT ALL HIS BENEFITS.`

segments.voice: Find three specific benefits you've received, not big abstract ones: a meal someone cooked, a body that got you out of bed, a friend who texted back. Say each one quietly, the way the psalm counts them, and sit with the list. If you pray, say the line, bless the Lord, O my soul; if you don't, let the three things sit there, remembered on purpose.
Lovingkindness. One of the benefits this psalm says God crowns us with, along with forgiveness, healing and a youth renewed like the eagle's.
Your line: forget not all his benefits. Wounds stay on file by themselves; kindnesses need a reminder. See you tomorrow.

432.title: The wild creation (Psalm 104)
432.hook: wine to gladden hearts, rocks for the badgers, a sea full of creatures
432.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians chant Psalm 104 at the opening of Vespers each evening, and many churches pray it at Pentecost and in services of thanksgiving for creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lovingkindness, a soul told not to forget, and your line, forget not all his benefits.

Lions roaring in the dark, asking for their dinner. Wild goats on cliffs too steep for anyone else. A stork nesting at the top of a fir tree. Donkeys drinking at a stream, birds singing in the branches above them. Then sunrise: the lions slink home to their dens, and a man heads out to work until evening. Out at sea, ships sail past an enormous creature that's simply playing in the waves. It sounds like the script for a nature documentary. It's a psalm, an ancient song of Israel, looking at the natural world for its own sake.
screen: `LIONS IN THE DARK.` → `GOATS ON THE CLIFFS.` → `A SEA CREATURE AT PLAY.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred four walks through creation roughly in the order of Genesis one: light, sky, waters, earth, plants, creatures, sun and moon. But where Genesis is spare, this psalm is crowded and noisy. Listen to verse eighteen in the King James Bible: "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies." Conies. The Hebrew is shaphan, usually identified as the rock hyrax: a small, furry, round animal that lives among rocks. Some translations call it a badger. Whatever you call it, God made the rocks for it. Not for us. That's the striking thing about this psalm. Humans show up as one creature among many. People get wine "that maketh glad the heart of man," and oil, and bread. Fine. But the lions get their meat from God too, and the storks get the fir trees. Then the sea: "There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein." Leviathan, the sea monster that frightens readers elsewhere in the Bible, made here to play. And the center of the psalm: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all." Some scholars hear echoes of an older Egyptian hymn to the sun in this psalm; if so, the psalmist took that wonder and turned it toward the one God. Orthodox Christians open their evening service, Vespers, with this psalm, and churches read it at Pentecost, for verse thirty: thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created.
screen: `GENESIS ONE, CROWDED AND NOISY` · `ROCKS FOR THE CONIES` · `LEVIATHAN, MADE TO PLAY` · `IN WISDOM HAST THOU MADE THEM ALL` · then, large: `O LORD, HOW MANIFOLD ARE THY WORKS!`

segments.voice: Look out a window, step outside, or call to mind one creature from the last few days, a pigeon, a spider in the corner, an ant on the counter, and watch it, or picture it. How does it move, what is it looking for, where will it sleep tonight? Don't call it useful or a nuisance; if you pray, say in wisdom hast thou made them all, and if you don't, simply watch.

Your line: all made in wisdom. Even the ones you'd shoo away. Four hundred thirty-two days, done.

433.title: I lift up my eyes (Psalm 121)
433.hook: a pilgrim's song: my help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth
433.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 121 before a journey, and it is often read at funerals and at services of blessing for travelers, pilgrims and people leaving home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leviathan, made to play, and your line, all made in wisdom.

Three times a year, the law of Moses called the people up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. For families far away that meant days on foot: dusty roads, children on shoulders, everyone singing to keep the pace. And the city sits high in the hills, so the last stretch is always uphill. Fifteen psalms in a row, one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty-four, carry the same heading in the King James Bible: A Song of degrees. Songs of going up. Some readers think pilgrims sang them on that road.
screen: `THREE FEASTS A YEAR.` → `THE ROAD GOES UPHILL.` → `SONGS OF GOING UP.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred twenty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." It reads like a statement: my help comes from the hills. But the Hebrew can just as easily be read as a question, and many translations print it that way: I lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? Why ask? The hills could be lovely, or they could be frightening. Bandits hid in them. Some readers think of hilltop shrines to other gods, offering help of their own. Either way, the pilgrim looks up, and the next line answers: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the voice changes. Someone else seems to answer the pilgrim, maybe a friend on the road, maybe a priest: "He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber." Suffer means allow. Your foot won't slip on the path. "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." The King James Bible switches between keep and preserve, so the English hides it, but in Hebrew it is one verb, shamar, six times in eight verses. The one who keeps watches your coming and going, by day and by night. And the last verse: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Some Christians pray this psalm before a journey.
screen: `A STATEMENT, OR A QUESTION?` · `NOT FROM THE HILLS` · `HE NEITHER SLUMBERS NOR SLEEPS` · `KEEP, SIX TIMES IN EIGHT VERSES` · then, large: `MY HELP COMETH FROM THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If you can see far, a skyline, a ridge, turn toward it and lift your eyes slowly, the way the pilgrim did; if you can't, picture the farthest place you've ever looked out over. Ask the pilgrim's question quietly: where does my help come from? 434.title: Like those who dream (Psalm 126)
434.hook: those who sow in tears shall reap in joy
434.carry: sow in tears, reap in joy
434.howItsDone: Christians often pray Psalm 126 in times of waiting and loss, and its sowing verse is sung in hymns such as "Bringing in the Sheaves"; Jewish families sing it before the grace after meals on Sabbaths and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shamar, keep, six times in eight verses, and your line, my help comes.

The phone rings. The scan came back clear. Or: the visa was approved. Or: they found him, he's safe. For a few seconds the person holding the phone can't take it in. A laugh comes out that's half crying. Say it again. News this good seems like the kind of thing you wake up from. Psalm one hundred twenty-six begins in exactly that moment, for a whole people. Something they had stopped expecting has happened, and the only word for it is a dream.
screen: `THE SCAN CAME BACK CLEAR.` → `SAY IT AGAIN.` → `IT FEELS LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Another song of going up, from the pilgrims' collection. In the King James Bible: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing." Some readers hear the return from exile in Babylon here, when the Persian king Cyrus let the deported families go home. Some scholars translate the Hebrew more broadly, as when the Lord restored the fortunes of Zion. Either way, the dreamers aren't asleep. They're wide awake, and it's too good to believe. Even the nations say: the Lord has done great things for them. Then, in verse four, the mood shifts. "Turn again our captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south." The south is the Negev, desert country. Its stream beds lie dry, until a heavy rain fills them with rushing water. So the people are asking for it again. The first homecoming wasn't the end of the hard part. Then the farmer's line: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him." Why would a farmer weep while sowing? Some readers picture a hungry year, when every handful of seed thrown into the ground is a handful you can't eat. Planting is an act of hope that costs something now. The psalm doesn't skip the tears. It promises the same farmer comes home with his arms full of sheaves. The gospel hymn Bringing in the Sheaves grew from this verse.
screen: `AWAKE, BUT IT FEELS LIKE A DREAM` · `STREAMS IN THE DRY SOUTH` · `SEED YOU COULD HAVE EATEN` · `SOW IN TEARS, BRING THE SHEAVES` · then, large: `THEY THAT SOW IN TEARS SHALL REAP IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Think of a hard place in your life, a dry stream bed, and choose one small seed to put into it: a kind word, a first step on something you've been putting off, a hope you've been too tired to name. Hold it the way a farmer holds seed before throwing it. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, just plant it on purpose.
Negev. The desert country in the south, whose dry streams suddenly rushing with rain is this psalm's picture of being restored.
Your line: sow in tears, reap in joy. That was this week in the Psalms: numbering our days, kanaf, a new song, lovingkindness, Leviathan, lifting our eyes, and the dreamers. See you tomorrow.
